name: Olive oil applied to the skin (massage, dressings)
short: In the nose: lipoid pneumonia in 5 children (cases). Skin: weaker barrier, mild redness (adults); less barrier-lipid gain (newborns); allergy cases. Colic, dialysis, foot-ulcer trials: no safety data.
text: This entry covers olive oil applied to the skin, including infant abdominal massage, plus one case series of olive oil put in the nose (a different route); it does not cover olive oil eaten as food. Skin barrier: in two randomised forearm studies in 19 adult volunteers with and without a history of atopic dermatitis, 4 weeks of olive oil significantly reduced stratum corneum integrity and caused mild redness; the authors say it therefore has the potential to promote and worsen atopic dermatitis and that its use for infant massage should be discouraged (this was not a study in infants). On the other side, in a within-person randomised trial in 54 healthy adults, extra virgin olive oil improved skin barrier function by increasing hydration and reducing redness, though only petrolatum reduced water loss through the skin. Infants: in a pilot randomised trial in 115 healthy full-term newborns, olive oil or sunflower oil twice daily for 4 weeks improved skin hydration but gave significantly less improvement in barrier-lipid structure than no oil, with no significant differences in water loss, pH or redness and skin scores; the trial was not powered for clinical outcomes, and the authors advise caution. A systematic review of skin care in healthy term babies says olive or sunflower oil for baby dry skin may adversely affect skin barrier function and found no evidence about baby massage; in a non-randomised study of 120 term newborns in intensive care, olive or almond oil caused no adverse effects on skin condition. The randomised trial of abdominal massage with olive oil in 80 infants aged 1 to 3 months with colic reports no adverse-event data. Nor do the abstracts of a 60-person trial of olive oil leg massage during haemodialysis, a 60-person trial of olive oil dressings on diabetic foot ulcers (its authors call the dressing safe, a verdict without event data), or a trial of a honey, beeswax and olive oil mixture in 39 people with atopic dermatitis or psoriasis; no cited source gives adverse-event data for olive oil applied to open wounds. Allergy and other skin reactions (case reports and patch-test studies): one report describes contact allergy to olive oil as rare, while another calls its 13 cases, identified from 1985 to 1989 in the dermatology departments of two hospitals, a high number; its title says those cases were in patients with venous eczema or were occupational, and in a masseur with occupational hand eczema the authors say external use of olive oil should be discouraged, at least in masseurs, under occlusion and in long-standing skin disease; in patch testing of 100 eczema patients, 5 had positive reactions but only 1 was probably allergic, and the authors describe olive oil as weakly irritant, more so under occlusion, and as less than suitable for treating venous insufficiency with eczema of the legs; one case of lichen planus pigmentosus improved only after a woman stopped applying olive oil all over her body. In adults: a meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials of olive oil to prevent pressure ulcers found no differences in adverse effects, and in a randomised study of 300 breastfeeding women, half of whom applied it to the nipples, no adverse effects occurred in mothers or newborns during its use. A different route: in a case series of 5 children aged 4 to 72 months from south-western Saudi Arabia, where olive oil is put into the noses of infants and children lying down to relieve congestion, the oil was aspirated into the lungs and caused lipoid pneumonia, which resolved with steroids and chest physiotherapy. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
